title: Emergent Biological Capabilities in a Foundation Model for Molecular Interactions
claim: Capabilities appear abruptly only at the largest scale, even though pretraining loss falls smoothly, so loss alone cannot predict emergence.
layout: 5 panels: top UMAP row of six scales, bottom row of four plots
description: The top row (panel A) shows six UMAP scatter plots, one for each model size from 42M to 1.6B parameters. Points are colored by mechanism-of-action class: inhibitor, activator, agonist, antagonist, substrate and product. The clusters are mixed at small scales and become separated, elongated streaks at 1.6B. A shared legend sits under the row. The bottom row has four line plots that all use log training FLOPs on the x-axis. B shows pretraining loss falling smoothly along a dotted power-law line, with a color gradient from light blue to red for the six scales. C (mechanism-of-action macro precision, yellow triangles), D (orthosteric vs. allosteric AUROC, blue squares) and E (covalent vs. non-covalent AUROC, red circles) stay flat or fluctuate near 0.6 and then jump sharply at 1.6B. The eye goes first to the colorful UMAPs, then to the steep final jumps.
caption: Capability emergence at scale. Controlled scaling experiment across six model scales (42M, 315M, 800M, 1B, 1.3B, 1.6B parameters) under identical conditions except parameter count. Panels (b) to (e) use log FLOPs as the x-axis. (a) UMAP projections (visualization only) of frozen interaction representations at each scale, colored by mechanism-of-action class. (b) Pretraining loss vs. training FLOPs. (c) Six-class mechanism-of-action macro precision from a parameter-free signature, mean over ten evaluation splits. (d) Zero-shot orthosteric vs. allosteric AUROC on 6,032 OOD complexes. Morgan fingerprint baseline shown dashed. (e) Zero-shot covalent vs. non-covalent AUROC on the OOD complexes in which neither class carries a detectable electrophilic warhead. All capability evaluations use parameter-free signatures derived from frozen representations and applied unchanged across scales.
abstract: Foundation models trained on large unlabeled corpora develop emergent capabilities, tasks that go beyond the training objective. We extend this paradigm to multimodal biology with Bonbon, a foundation model for molecular interactions trained on approximately 3.2 trillion tokens of paired protein-ligand sequences. From a single representation space, Bonbon exhibits three zero-shot emergent capabilities at hierarchical levels of resolution: functional (mechanism of action), residue (binding site localization, including orthosteric/allosteric discrimination), and bond (covalent versus non-covalent engagement). All three capabilities generalize to out-of-distribution complexes. Bonbon was trained on protein-ligand sequences alone, without any task-specific supervision and without structural coordinates. We conducted controlled scaling experiments across six model scales from 42M to 1.6B parameters; every capability evaluated shows a sharp jump at the largest scale on continuous metrics, even as pretraining loss decreases smoothly. This demonstrates that loss-based scaling laws alone are insufficient to predict when zero-shot emergent capabilities become available. The capabilities reported here emerge after training at a 1:2,000 parameter-to-token ratio to accommodate the sparsity of paired biological interaction data. The same frozen representations achieve state-of-the-art binding and affinity prediction at five orders of magnitude greater speed than co-folding methods. In prospective wet-lab validation across nine disease targets spanning seven protein families, Bonbon achieves a 61.5% dose-response hit rate on de novo compounds, yielding structurally novel molecules not previously reported to inhibit these proteins, including for out-of-distribution targets.
